claim: Members of the Tolloid family of metalloproteinases liberate BMPs from inhibitory complexes to regulate BMP gradient formation during embryonic dorsal-ventral axis patterning.
source: Members of the Tolloid family of metalloproteinases liberate BMPs from inhibitory complexes to regulate BMP gradient formation during embryonic dorsal-ventral axis patterning.
evidence: This is a general statement about Tolloid function supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: Tolloid, via its N-terminal CUB domains, interacts with Collagen IV.
source: We show that Tolloid, via its N-terminal CUB domains, interacts with Collagen IV, which enhances Tolloid activity towards its substrate Sog, and facilitates Tsg-dependent stimulation of cleavage.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including binding assays and deletion studies shown in Figure 4.

claim: The Tolloid-Collagen IV interaction enhances Tolloid activity towards its substrate Sog.
source: We show that Tolloid, via its N-terminal CUB domains, interacts with Collagen IV, which enhances Tolloid activity towards its substrate Sog, and facilitates Tsg-dependent stimulation of cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by cleavage assays shown in Figure 4C demonstrating increased Sog processing in the presence of Collagen IV.

claim: The Tolloid-Collagen IV interaction facilitates Tsg-dependent stimulation of cleavage.
source: We show that Tolloid, via its N-terminal CUB domains, interacts with Collagen IV, which enhances Tolloid activity towards its substrate Sog, and facilitates Tsg-dependent stimulation of cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing that Tsg enhancement requires Collagen IV binding.

claim: The two most C-terminal Tld CUB domains mediate Sog interaction to facilitate its processing.
source: In contrast, the two most C-terminal Tld CUB domains mediate Sog interaction to facilitate its processing as, based on our structural data, Tolloid curvature positions bound Sog in proximity to the protease domain.
evidence: This is supported by deletion studies and binding assays shown in Figure 2D demonstrating that CUB4 and CUB5 deletions lose Sog binding.

claim: Tolloid curvature positions bound Sog in proximity to the protease domain.
source: In contrast, the two most C-terminal Tld CUB domains mediate Sog interaction to facilitate its processing as, based on our structural data, Tolloid curvature positions bound Sog in proximity to the protease domain.
evidence: This is inferred from structural data shown in Figure 1, including SAXS and EM models showing Tld curvature.

claim: Artificially tethering the Tld protease domain to Sog can recapitulate embryonic BMP gradient formation in the absence of Tolloid non-catalytic domains.
source: Having ascribed functions to the Tolloid non-catalytic domains, we recapitulate embryonic BMP gradient formation in their absence, by artificially tethering the Tld protease domain to Sog.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo rescue experiments shown in Figure 6D demonstrating restoration of BMP target gene expression.

claim: A heterodimer of the BMP ligands, Dpp and Scw, acts as the most potent BMP signalling species in the early Drosophila embryo.
source: The mechanism of BMP gradient formation has been extensively studied in the early Drosophila embryo, where a heterodimer of the BMP ligands, Dpp and Scw, acts as the most potent BMP signalling species (Shimmi et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shimmi et al., 2005.

claim: In dorsolateral regions, an inhibitory complex is formed with the Dpp-Scw heterodimer bound by the extracellular antagonists Sog and Tsg.
source: In dorsolateral regions, an inhibitory complex is formed, with the Dpp-Scw heterodimer bound by the extracellular antagonists Sog and Tsg (Wharton and Serpe, 2013), aided by the scaffold protein Collagen IV (Wang et al., 2008; Sawala et al., 2012; Wharton and Serpe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Collagen IV aids in the formation of the inhibitory complex containing Dpp-Scw, Sog, and Tsg.
source: In dorsolateral regions, an inhibitory complex is formed, with the Dpp-Scw heterodimer bound by the extracellular antagonists Sog and Tsg (Wharton and Serpe, 2013), aided by the scaffold protein Collagen IV (Wang et al., 2008; Sawala et al., 2012; Wharton and Serpe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2008 and Sawala et al., 2012.

claim: In the inhibitory complex, the Dpp-Scw heterodimer is unable to bind to receptors or Collagen IV.
source: In this inhibitory complex, the Dpp-Scw heterodimer is unable to bind to receptors or Collagen IV, but is free to diffuse dorsally.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of the inhibitory complex function.

claim: The secreted Tld metalloproteinase cleaves Sog to release active BMP ligand.
source: The secreted Tld metalloproteinase cleaves Sog to release active BMP ligand, however in dorsolateral regions due to the high concentration of Sog, the ligand dimer is rebound.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Tld function in BMP gradient formation.

claim: Through a cycle of complex formation, diffusion and cleavage, BMP ligands accumulate at the dorsal midline.
source: Thus it is through a cycle of complex formation, diffusion and cleavage that the ligands accumulate at the dorsal midline where, upon cleavage by Tld, Dpp-Scw is free to signal (Wharton and Serpe, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wharton and Serpe, 2013.

claim: A second phase of gradient formation involving intracellular positive feedback refines the initial broad Dpp-Scw gradient into a peak of BMP receptor activation at the dorsal midline.
source: A second phase of gradient formation involving intracellular positive feedback then refines this initial broad Dpp-Scw gradient into a peak of BMP receptor activation at the dorsal midline (Wang and Ferguson, 2005; Gavin-Smyth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang and Ferguson, 2005 and Gavin-Smyth et al., 2013.

claim: Enzymes within the Tld family have a well-characterised domain structure in which the N-terminal protease domain is followed by a series of non-catalytic CUB and EGF domains.
source: Enzymes within the Tld family have a well-characterised domain structure in which the N-terminal protease domain is followed by a series of non-catalytic CUB (Complement-Uegf-BMP1) and EGF (Epidermal Growth Factor-like) domains (Muir and Greenspan, 2011) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Muir and Greenspan, 2011 and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mammalian Tolloid (mTld) and Tolloid-like-1 (Tll-1) form dimers.
source: Structural analysis of mammalian Tolloids has revealed that both mammalian Tolloid (mTld) and Tolloid-like-1 (Tll-1) form dimers in which the most C-terminal EGF and CUB domains act in a substrate exclusion mechanism to restrict enzyme activity (Berry et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2009 and 2010.

claim: In mammalian Tolloid and Tolloid-like-1 dimers, the most C-terminal EGF and CUB domains act in a substrate exclusion mechanism to restrict enzyme activity.
source: Structural analysis of mammalian Tolloids has revealed that both mammalian Tolloid (mTld) and Tolloid-like-1 (Tll-1) form dimers in which the most C-terminal EGF and CUB domains act in a substrate exclusion mechanism to restrict enzyme activity (Berry et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2009 and 2010.

claim: The highly active, shorter BMP1 protease is monomeric.
source: In contrast, the highly active, shorter BMP1 protease is monomeric (Berry et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Berry et al., 2009.

claim: Removing the three most C-terminal domains from Drosophila Tld to mimic a shorter BMP1-like form results in a loss of activity.
source: Although Drosophila Tld possesses a similar domain structure to mTld, previous studies suggest that removing the three most C-terminal domains, to mimic a shorter BMP1-like form, results in a loss of activity (Canty et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Canty et al., 2006.

claim: A substrate exclusion mechanism may not exist for Drosophila Tld.
source: Therefore, a substrate exclusion mechanism may not exist for Drosophila Tld.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that removing C-terminal domains reduces rather than increases activity.

claim: Single amino acid mutations in four out of the five CUB domains result in some degree of ventralisation of the Drosophila embryo.
source: In addition, despite single amino acid mutations in four out of the five CUB domains resulting in some degree of ventralisation of the Drosophila embryo, the requirement for these domains in Drosophila Tld function is unclear (Ferguson and Anderson, 1992; Childs and O'Connor, 1994; Finelli et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferguson and Anderson, 1992; Childs and O'Connor, 1994; Finelli et al., 1994.

claim: Drosophila Tld has a maximal particle dimension (Dmax) of 17.7 nm.
source: Drosophila Tld has a maximal particle dimension (Dmax) of 17.7 nm and a radius of gyration (Rg) of 4.6 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Drosophila Tld has a radius of gyration (Rg) of 4.6 nm.
source: Drosophila Tld has a maximal particle dimension (Dmax) of 17.7 nm and a radius of gyration (Rg) of 4.6 nm (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on SAXS data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ab initio modelling of Drosophila Tld gives an elongated monomer with the approximate dimensions 18 × 6.5 × 6.8 nm.
source: Ab inito modelling of the most probable shape of Drosophila Tld gives an elongated monomer with the approximate dimensions 18 × 6.5 × 6.8 nm (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on SAXS ab initio modeling shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Drosophila Tld displays an elongated conformation with protein curvature around the C-terminal tail.
source: An overlay of the ab inito model and rigid body model (Figure 1C) shows that Tld displays an elongated conformation with protein curvature around the C-terminal tail (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: The curvature of Drosophila Tld brings the most C-terminal CUB domains into close proximity to the N-terminal protease domain.
source: This brings the most C-terminal CUB domains into close proximity to the N-terminal protease domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing Tld curvature in Figure 1D.

claim: Single particle analysis TEM demonstrates that Drosophila Tld is a monomer.
source: Single particle analysis TEM demonstrates that Drosophila Tld is a monomer, with the overall shape of the 3D reconstruction in agreement with the SAXS model (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on TEM data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The overall shape of the Drosophila Tld 3D reconstruction from TEM is in agreement with the SAXS model.
source: Single particle analysis TEM demonstrates that Drosophila Tld is a monomer, with the overall shape of the 3D reconstruction in agreement with the SAXS model (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on comparison of TEM and SAXS data shown in Figures 1E, 1F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The curvature of the TEM model mimics that seen in the rigid body model.
source: In addition to being relatively elongated, the curvature of the EM model mimics that seen in the RBM (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on comparison shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The TEM model is shorter than the SAXS model, suggesting flexibility of the most C-terminal regions.
source: However, it is evident that the TEM model is shorter; this suggests flexibility of the most C-terminal regions that is likely to result in loss of information on this region during the averaging procedure.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of TEM and SAXS models.

claim: Cleavage of Sog by Tld relies on the presence of Dpp.
source: Cleavage of Sog by Tld relies on the presence of Dpp (Marques et al., 1997) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as such Dpp was added to all in vitro assays.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marques et al., 1997 and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only ΔCUB2 retained the ability to cleave Sog among the CUB domain deletion variants tested.
source: Only ΔCUB2 retained the ability to cleave Sog, although the level of cleavage by ΔCUB2 is lower than full-length Tld (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: The level of cleavage by ΔCUB2 is lower than full-length Tld.
source: Only ΔCUB2 retained the ability to cleave Sog, although the level of cleavage by ΔCUB2 is lower than full-length Tld (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Increasing levels of Tsg enhance Tld cleavage of the Sog 50 and 33 kDa fragments, especially the 33 kDa fragment.
source: Additionally, whilst increasing levels of Tsg enhances Tld cleavage of the Sog 50 and 33 kDa fragments, especially the 33 kDa fragment as described previously (Shimmi and O'Connor, 2003), ΔCUB2 mediated cleavage is not enhanced (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shimmi and O'Connor, 2003 and data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ΔCUB2 mediated cleavage is not enhanced by Tsg.
source: Additionally, whilst increasing levels of Tsg enhances Tld cleavage of the Sog 50 and 33 kDa fragments, especially the 33 kDa fragment as described previously (Shimmi and O'Connor, 2003), ΔCUB2 mediated cleavage is not enhanced (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CUB2 is not required for Tld activity.
source: Therefore, while CUB2 is not required for Tld activity, its presence is necessary for Tsg enhancement of cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ΔCUB2 retains cleavage activity.

claim: CUB2 is necessary for Tsg enhancement of cleavage.
source: Therefore, while CUB2 is not required for Tld activity, its presence is necessary for Tsg enhancement of cleavage.
evidence: This is based on the observation that ΔCUB2 cleavage is not enhanced by Tsg, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The isolated metalloproteinase domain and CUB4 and CUB5 deletions are unable to interact with Sog.
source: Analysis of Sog–Tld interactions reveals that, similar to the isolated protease domain, the CUB4 and CUB5 deletions are unable to interact with Sog, suggesting that these domains mediate Sog interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: CUB4 and CUB5 domains mediate Sog interaction.
source: Analysis of Sog–Tld interactions reveals that, similar to the isolated protease domain, the CUB4 and CUB5 deletions are unable to interact with Sog, suggesting that these domains mediate Sog interaction (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Sog binding when CUB4 or CUB5 are deleted, shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Full-length variants of Tld with CUB4 or CUB5 domain duplications at the C-terminus are inactive.
source: However, these enzymes are also inactive, demonstrating a specific requirement for the CUB4–CUB5 domain pair at the C-terminus of Tld (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a specific requirement for the CUB4–CUB5 domain pair at the C-terminus of Tld.
source: However, these enzymes are also inactive, demonstrating a specific requirement for the CUB4–CUB5 domain pair at the C-terminus of Tld (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the inactivity of CUB4 or CUB5 duplication variants shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: ΔCUB2 interacts with Sog to a similar extent as wildtype Tld.
source: For the other single CUB deletions, ΔCUB2 interacts with Sog to a similar extent as wildtype Tld even though its activity is reduced and, despite being inactive, the ΔCUB1 and ΔCUB3 forms can bind Sog, albeit at reduced levels (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ΔCUB1 and ΔCUB3 forms can bind Sog, albeit at reduced levels.
source: For the other single CUB deletions, ΔCUB2 interacts with Sog to a similar extent as wildtype Tld even though its activity is reduced and, despite being inactive, the ΔCUB1 and ΔCUB3 forms can bind Sog, albeit at reduced levels (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A correct protein conformation is important for Tld activity.
source: These data suggest that a correct protein conformation is important for Tld activity, or that CUB1 and CUB3 mediate a different protein interaction that is important for Sog binding (see later).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ΔCUB1 and ΔCUB3 can bind Sog but are inactive.

claim: CUB1 and CUB3 may mediate a different protein interaction that is important for Sog binding.
source: These data suggest that a correct protein conformation is important for Tld activity, or that CUB1 and CUB3 mediate a different protein interaction that is important for Sog binding (see later).
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation that ΔCUB1 and ΔCUB3 show reduced Sog binding and activity.

claim: In tldE839K homozygous mutant embryos, expression of the peak threshold gene Race is lost.
source: Visualisation of the expression patterns of the Dpp target genes Race and u-shaped (ush) in tldE839K homozygous mutant embryos reveals that expression of the peak threshold gene Race is lost and expression of the lower threshold gene ush is narrower than in wild-type embryos (Figure 3B), suggesting shallow gradient formation, consistent with the previous characterisation of this allele as weak.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In tldE839K homozygous mutant embryos, expression of the lower threshold gene ush is narrower than in wild-type embryos.
source: Visualisation of the expression patterns of the Dpp target genes Race and u-shaped (ush) in tldE839K homozygous mutant embryos reveals that expression of the peak threshold gene Race is lost and expression of the lower threshold gene ush is narrower than in wild-type embryos (Figure 3B), suggesting shallow gradient formation, consistent with the previous characterisation of this allele as weak.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The tldE839K phenotype suggests shallow gradient formation.
source: Visualisation of the expression patterns of the Dpp target genes Race and u-shaped (ush) in tldE839K homozygous mutant embryos reveals that expression of the peak threshold gene Race is lost and expression of the lower threshold gene ush is narrower than in wild-type embryos (Figure 3B), suggesting shallow gradient formation, consistent with the previous characterisation of this allele as weak.
evidence: This is inferred from the loss of Race and narrowing of ush expression shown in Figure 3B.

claim: All four mutated residues in CUB4 and CUB5 lie on the surface of the protein.
source: Identification of the positions of the four mutated residues within the individual CUB domain structures reveals that all lie on the surface of the protein (Figure 3C) and therefore can by hypothesised to be important for substrate binding.
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The four mutated residues in CUB4 and CUB5 can be hypothesised to be important for substrate binding.
source: Identification of the positions of the four mutated residues within the individual CUB domain structures reveals that all lie on the surface of the protein (Figure 3C) and therefore can by hypothesised to be important for substrate binding.
evidence: This is speculated based on their surface position shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Each CUB4/5 point mutant shows reduced binding to Sog.
source: Each mutant shows reduced binding to Sog (Figure 3D) and a loss of cleavage activity when tested over a short reaction time (Figure 3Ei), although upon a longer incubation time varying levels of weaker cleavage activity can be detected for all of the mutant Tld proteins tested (Figure 3Eii).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Each CUB4/5 point mutant shows a loss of cleavage activity when tested over a short reaction time.
source: Each mutant shows reduced binding to Sog (Figure 3D) and a loss of cleavage activity when tested over a short reaction time (Figure 3Ei), although upon a longer incubation time varying levels of weaker cleavage activity can be detected for all of the mutant Tld proteins tested (Figure 3Eii).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3Ei.

claim: Upon a longer incubation time, varying levels of weaker cleavage activity can be detected for all of the CUB4/5 mutant Tld proteins tested.
source: Each mutant shows reduced binding to Sog (Figure 3D) and a loss of cleavage activity when tested over a short reaction time (Figure 3Ei), although upon a longer incubation time varying levels of weaker cleavage activity can be detected for all of the mutant Tld proteins tested (Figure 3Eii).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3Eii.

claim: The molecular defect underlying the CUB4/5 point mutations is reduced binding to Sog.
source: Together, these data provide molecular understanding of how these mutations impair Tld activity, and provide in vivo support for the importance of CUB4 and CUB5 in mediating the Tld–Sog interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced Sog binding and cleavage activity of the mutants shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Collagen IV was identified as a Tld binding protein in a pilot mass spectrometry screen.
source: In a pilot mass spectrometry screen for Tld binding proteins we identified Collagen IV, an extracellular matrix protein that we have previously shown to be required for Dpp gradient formation (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data and citation to Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Collagen IV is required for Dpp gradient formation.
source: In a pilot mass spectrometry screen for Tld binding proteins we identified Collagen IV, an extracellular matrix protein that we have previously shown to be required for Dpp gradient formation (Wang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2008.

claim: Tld binds to Collagen IV via its N-terminal CUB domains.
source: Tld binds to Collagen IV via its N-terminal CUB domains, with deletion of CUB1, CUB2 or CUB3 reducing binding to <25% that of full-length (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Deletion of CUB1, CUB2 or CUB3 reduces Tld binding to Collagen IV to <25% that of full-length.
source: Tld binds to Collagen IV via its N-terminal CUB domains, with deletion of CUB1, CUB2 or CUB3 reducing binding to <25% that of full-length (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Removal of the Sog interacting domains, CUB4 and CUB5, has little effect on the Tld-Collagen IV interaction.
source: However, removal of the Sog interacting domains, CUB4 and CUB5, has little effect on the Tld-Collagen IV interaction.
evidence: This is based on pulldown assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Addition of the NC1 domains from both Drosophila Collagen IV proteins, Vkg and Dcg1, increases the Sog–Tld interaction.
source: To test the effect of Collagen IV on Tld and Sog interaction, their binding was investigated in the presence of an increased amount of Collagen IV. Addition of the NC1 domains from both Drosophila Collagen IV proteins, Vkg and Dcg1, increases the Sog–Tld interaction (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The addition of Collagen IV enhances Tld cleavage at both the 50 and 33 kDa sites of Sog.
source: The addition of Collagen IV enhances Tld cleavage at both the 50 and 33 kDa sites of Sog (Figure 4C), consistent with increased Sog–Tld interaction in the presence of Collagen IV (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The addition of Tsg increases Sog cleavage, especially at the 33 kDa site in the presence of Collagen IV.
source: The addition of Tsg increases Sog cleavage, especially at the 33 kDa site in the presence of Collagen IV.
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Collagen IV enhancement of Sog processing is reduced in the presence of high levels of Tsg.
source: However, the Collagen IV enhancement of Sog processing is reduced in the presence of high levels of Tsg (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Little enhancement at either the 50 or 33 kDa site is observed in the presence of Collagen IV when the ΔCUB2 mutant is tested.
source: In contrast, little enhancement at either the 50 or 33 kDa site is observed in the presence of Collagen IV when the ΔCUB2 mutant, that is defective in Collagen IV interaction, is tested (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Tsg fails to enhance Sog processing by the ΔCUB2 mutant.
source: As before (Figure 2C), Tsg fails to enhance Sog processing by the ΔCUB2 mutant (Figure 4C), suggesting that Tsg function may depend on a Tld-Collagen IV interaction.
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Tsg function may depend on a Tld-Collagen IV interaction.
source: As before (Figure 2C), Tsg fails to enhance Sog processing by the ΔCUB2 mutant (Figure 4C), suggesting that Tsg function may depend on a Tld-Collagen IV interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of Tsg enhancement with ΔCUB2 shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Tld binding to Collagen IV enhances the Sog-Tld interaction and Sog cleavage.
source: These data show that Tld binding to Collagen IV enhances the Sog-Tld interaction and Sog cleavage.
evidence: This is based on the combined data from Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: SogCR14* is a much poorer substrate for Tld cleavage compared to wildtype Sog.
source: This mutant Sog is a much poorer substrate for Tld cleavage compared to wildtype Sog, and no enhancement of cleavage in the presence of added Collagen IV is observed (Figure 4D), contrary to that observed with wildtype Sog (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No enhancement of SogCR14* cleavage in the presence of added Collagen IV is observed.
source: This mutant Sog is a much poorer substrate for Tld cleavage compared to wildtype Sog, and no enhancement of cleavage in the presence of added Collagen IV is observed (Figure 4D), contrary to that observed with wildtype Sog (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: There is very little of the 33 kDa cleavage fragment from SogCR14*, even when Tsg is added in increasing amounts.
source: In addition, there is very little of the 33 kDa cleavage fragment, even when Tsg is added in increasing amounts (Figure 4D), suggesting that Tsg function requires a Sog-Collagen IV interaction, in addition to a Tld-Collagen IV interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tsg function requires a Sog-Collagen IV interaction, in addition to a Tld-Collagen IV interaction.
source: In addition, there is very little of the 33 kDa cleavage fragment, even when Tsg is added in increasing amounts (Figure 4D), suggesting that Tsg function requires a Sog-Collagen IV interaction, in addition to a Tld-Collagen IV interaction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of 33 kDa fragment production from SogCR14* shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The SogCR14* mutant accumulates to a greater level than the wildtype Sog in vivo.
source: Consistent with SogCR14* being a poorer Tld substrate in vitro, analysis of embryos expressing either wildtype Sog or the SogCR14* double mutant under the control of the sog lateral stripe (ls) enhancer reveals that the SogCR14* mutant accumulates to a greater level than the wildtype Sog in vivo (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence and Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding of both Sog and Tld to Collagen IV is necessary for efficient Sog processing.
source: Together these data show that binding of both Sog and Tld to Collagen IV is necessary for efficient Sog processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing reduced processing when either Sog or Tld cannot bind Collagen IV.

claim: All CUB2/3 point mutants show reduced Collagen IV binding by at least two-fold.
source: The mutations were engineered into Tld-HA and we first tested for Collagen IV binding, which is reduced by at least two-fold in all CUB2/3 point mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on pulldown assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All CUB2/3 point mutants show reduced Sog interaction.
source: We next tested the effect of these point mutations on Sog interaction. All Tld mutants show reduced Sog interaction, with the same severity profile as that observed for the defects in Collagen IV binding (Figure 5Di,iii, cf with Figure 5Cii), consistent with the data presented in Figure 4 that Collagen IV promotes the Tld–Sog interaction.
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The severity profile of Sog interaction defects for CUB2/3 mutants is the same as that observed for the defects in Collagen IV binding.
source: We next tested the effect of these point mutations on Sog interaction. All Tld mutants show reduced Sog interaction, with the same severity profile as that observed for the defects in Collagen IV binding (Figure 5Di,iii, cf with Figure 5Cii), consistent with the data presented in Figure 4 that Collagen IV promotes the Tld–Sog interaction.
evidence: This is based on comparison of data in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: The four CUB2/3 mutant Tld proteins all show equivalent levels of binding to SogCR14* as that observed for wildtype Tld.
source: However, the four mutant Tld proteins all show equivalent levels of binding to this form of Sog, as that observed for wildtype Tld (Figure 5Dii,iii).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5Dii,iii.

claim: The CUB2/3 mutations do not affect Sog interaction per se, but rather disrupt the stimulatory effect observed through Collagen IV.
source: These data reveal that the CUB2/3 mutations do not affect Sog interaction per se, but rather disrupt the stimulatory effect observed through Collagen IV.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that CUB2/3 mutants bind SogCR14* normally but show reduced binding to wildtype Sog.

claim: The four CUB2/3 mutant Tld proteins show reduced cleavage of Sog, especially of the 33 kDa fragment.
source: In terms of cleavage activity, the four mutant Tld proteins show reduced cleavage of Sog, especially of the 33 kDa fragment (Figure 5E), consistent with their reduced ability to bind Sog and the requirement for Collagen IV for Tsg enhancement of processing at the 33 kDa site.
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The molecular defect underlying the phenotypes associated with the CUB2/3 point mutations is a weak ability to bind Collagen IV.
source: Together, these data suggest that the molecular defect underlying the phenotypes associated with the CUB2/3 point mutations is a weak ability to bind Collagen IV.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data showing reduced Collagen IV binding and consequent effects on Sog processing.

claim: SogZ+ specifically interacts with the corresponding MPZ− zipper but not the MPZ+ or unmodified MP domain controls.
source: Immunoprecipitations confirmed the ability of the leucine zippers to induce enzyme-substrate interaction; SogZ+ specifically interacts with the corresponding MPZ− zipper but not the MPZ+ or unmodified MP domain controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both full-length Tld and MPZ− cleave SogZ+ to yield two cleavage fragments at 57 kDa and 40 kDa.
source: To test whether the interaction induced by the leucine zippers is sufficient to rescue the activity of the isolated protease domain, cleavage assays were carried out in cell culture. Both full-length Tld and MPZ− cleave SogZ+ to yield two cleavage fragments at 57 kDa and 40 kDa (Figure 6C), equivalent to the 50 and 33 kDa fragments plus the additional zipper sequence.
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Using the artificial zipper system, Sog and the Tld MP domain can interact in the absence of Dpp.
source: Using this artificial system, Sog and the Tld MP domain can interact in the absence of Dpp, although Dpp still enhances SogZ+ cleavage (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Dpp still enhances SogZ+ cleavage in the zipper system.
source: Using this artificial system, Sog and the Tld MP domain can interact in the absence of Dpp, although Dpp still enhances SogZ+ cleavage (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: In a tld null background with expression of either SogZ+ or MPZ− but not both, Race and ush expression are lost.
source: In a tld null background with expression of either SogZ+ or MPZ− but not both, Race and ush expression are lost (Figure 6Dii, cf Figure 6Di).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6Dii.

claim: When tld null mutant embryos express both SogZ+ and MPZ−, target gene expression is rescued in 50% of cases.
source: In contrast, when tld null mutant embryos express both SogZ+ and MPZ−, target gene expression is rescued in 50% of cases (Figure 6Diii), although ∼20% of the rescued embryos show a slight thinning of Race expression in the central region of the embryo, as observed for the addition of an extra copy of ls-sogZ+ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6Diii.

claim: Approximately 20% of the rescued embryos show a slight thinning of Race expression in the central region of the embryo.
source: In contrast, when tld null mutant embryos express both SogZ+ and MPZ−, target gene expression is rescued in 50% of cases (Figure 6Diii), although ∼20% of the rescued embryos show a slight thinning of Race expression in the central region of the embryo, as observed for the addition of an extra copy of ls-sogZ+ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6Diii and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Artificial tethering of the MP domain to Sog can be sufficient for BMP gradient formation in vivo.
source: Overall, these findings indicate that this artificial tethering of the MP domain to Sog can be sufficient for BMP gradient formation in vivo.
evidence: This is based on the rescue data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Drosophila Tld is a monomer.
source: Our biophysical data provide evidence that Tld is a monomer, which efficiently cleaves Sog due to critical bipartite functions of the Tld non-catalytic domains in either substrate or ECM interaction.
evidence: This is based on SAXS and TEM data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Tld efficiently cleaves Sog due to critical bipartite functions of the Tld non-catalytic domains in either substrate or ECM interaction.
source: Our biophysical data provide evidence that Tld is a monomer, which efficiently cleaves Sog due to critical bipartite functions of the Tld non-catalytic domains in either substrate or ECM interaction.
evidence: This is based on the combined experimental data from binding and cleavage assays.

claim: Tld represents the first five CUB domain family member that exists as a monomer.
source: Thus, Tld represents the first five CUB domain family member that exists as a monomer, as Tll-1 and mTld have previously been shown to be dimers that exclude Chordin substrate resulting in low catalytic activity towards it (Berry et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: This is based on comparison with previous structural studies of mammalian Tolloids cited.

claim: Tll-1 and mTld have previously been shown to be dimers that exclude Chordin substrate resulting in low catalytic activity towards it.
source: Thus, Tld represents the first five CUB domain family member that exists as a monomer, as Tll-1 and mTld have previously been shown to be dimers that exclude Chordin substrate resulting in low catalytic activity towards it (Berry et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Berry et al., 2009 and 2010.

claim: Dimeric Tolloids require the affinity of substrate interaction to be higher than the intramolecular affinity within the dimer for activation.
source: Thus, whereas the dimeric Tolloids require the affinity of substrate interaction to be higher than the intramolecular affinity within the dimer for activation (Hintze et al., 2006; Berry et al., 2009), this is not a limitation for Drosophila Tld.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hintze et al., 2006 and Berry et al., 2009.

claim: The substrate exclusion mechanism is not a limitation for Drosophila Tld.
source: Thus, whereas the dimeric Tolloids require the affinity of substrate interaction to be higher than the intramolecular affinity within the dimer for activation (Hintze et al., 2006; Berry et al., 2009), this is not a limitation for Drosophila Tld.
evidence: This is inferred from Drosophila Tld being monomeric.

claim: An interaction has been identified between Collagen IV and the CUB domains of PCPE-1.
source: Consistent with this, recently an interaction has been identified between Collagen IV and the CUB domains of PCPE-1 (Salza et al., 2014), and Collagen IV binds the zebrafish G-protein coupled receptor GPR126, via a region containing the CUB domain (Paavola et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Salza et al., 2014.

claim: Collagen IV binds the zebrafish G-protein coupled receptor GPR126, via a region containing the CUB domain.
source: Consistent with this, recently an interaction has been identified between Collagen IV and the CUB domains of PCPE-1 (Salza et al., 2014), and Collagen IV binds the zebrafish G-protein coupled receptor GPR126, via a region containing the CUB domain (Paavola et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Paavola et al., 2014.

claim: Sog and Dpp-Scw bind independently to Collagen IV.
source: In addition to Sog and Dpp-Scw, which have been previously shown to bind independently to Collagen IV (Sawala et al., 2012), the data presented here show that Tld, via its CUB1-3 domains, also binds to Collagen IV (Figure 7, step 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawala et al., 2012.

claim: When Dpp-Scw is transferred to Sog from Collagen IV, Tld is transferred at the same time, interacting with Sog via the Tld CUB4 and CUB5 domains.
source: However, in the next step, when Dpp-Scw is transferred to Sog from Collagen IV, as has been previously described (Sawala et al., 2012), we suggest that Tld is transferred at the same time, interacting with Sog via the Tld CUB4 and CUB5 domains (Figure 7, step 2).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and shown in Figure 7.

claim: Tsg releases Dpp-Scw/Sog from Collagen IV as a Dpp-Scw/Tsg complex.
source: Tsg has previously been shown to release Dpp-Scw/Sog from Collagen IV as a Dpp-Scw/Tsg complex (Wang et al., 2008), with Tsg recruitment or interaction potentially stabilised by the BMP binding capacity of Tsg's N-terminal domain (Oelgeschlager et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2008 and Oelgeschlager et al., 2000.

claim: Tld is released from Collagen IV at the same time as the Dpp-Scw/Tsg complex, pre-bound to the shuttling complex.
source: Therefore, based on the data obtained here, we suggest that in addition Tld is released from Collagen IV at the same time, pre-bound to the shuttling complex (Figure 7, step 3), and is then able to fully process Sog (step 4).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The enhancement of Tld cleavage of Sog in the presence of Collagen IV is due to Collagen IV acting as a scaffold to promote Tld interaction with Sog.
source: The model predicts that the enhancement of Tld cleavage of Sog that we observe in the presence of Collagen IV is due to Collagen IV acting as a scaffold to promote Tld interaction with Sog.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing enhanced Tld-Sog interaction and cleavage in the presence of Collagen IV.

claim: When Tsg is in excess, there is little Sog binding to Collagen IV, so the positive effect of Collagen IV is reduced.
source: As Tsg has been suggested previously to compete with Collagen IV for binding to the SogCR1 domain to release the Sog-BMP complex from Collagen IV (Sawala et al., 2012), it is possible that there is little Sog binding to Collagen IV when Tsg is in excess, so the positive effect of Collagen IV is reduced.
evidence: This is speculated based on previous findings and the current data.

claim: The BMP dependency for Sog cleavage by Tld arises from the requirement for Dpp-Scw to disrupt the SogCR4-Collagen IV interaction.
source: In the model presented, the BMP dependency for Sog cleavage by Tld arises from the requirement for Dpp-Scw to disrupt the SogCR4-Collagen IV interaction as described previously (Sawala et al., 2012), resulting in an 'opening' of Sog that facilitates Tld binding.
evidence: This is based on the model and supported by citation to Sawala et al., 2012.

claim: Tld is unable to bind to Sog in the absence of Dpp.
source: In support of this, we find that Tld is unable to bind to Sog in the absence of Dpp (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations mentioned in the text.

claim: Tld levels are not limiting in the Drosophila embryo.
source: Although Tld levels are not limiting in the Drosophila embryo (Eldar et al., 2002), it is possible that Tld activity is suboptimal in order to allow sufficient diffusion required for peak gradient formation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eldar et al., 2002.

claim: Tld activity may be suboptimal in order to allow sufficient diffusion required for peak gradient formation.
source: Although Tld levels are not limiting in the Drosophila embryo (Eldar et al., 2002), it is possible that Tld activity is suboptimal in order to allow sufficient diffusion required for peak gradient formation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the mechanism of gradient formation.

claim: Mathematical modelling has revealed that lowering Tld processing activity favours a more defined BMP peak, due to an increase in BMP shuttling to the dorsal midline.
source: Consistent with this idea, mathematical modelling has revealed that lowering Tld processing activity favours a more defined BMP peak, due to an increase in BMP shuttling to the dorsal midline (Peluso et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peluso et al., 2011.

claim: A recent model of BMP shuttling in the sea urchin embryo finds Tld to be a dominant determinant of the system.
source: In addition, a recent model of BMP shuttling in the sea urchin embryo finds Tld to be a dominant determinant of the system, with reduced levels of Tld relative to the fly system necessary for the best fit to the spatial extent of the BMP signalling peak in sea urchins (van Heijster et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to van Heijster et al., 2014.

claim: In the absence of Collagen IV, or the binding of Sog or Tld to it, there is little Tsg enhancement of Sog cleavage and liberation of the 33 kDa fragment.
source: In the absence of Collagen IV, or the binding of Sog or Tld to it, we observe little Tsg enhancement of Sog cleavage and liberation of the 33 kDa fragment.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: All of the CUB2/3 point mutants are more severely compromised in their ability to cleave the 33 kDa site, compared to the 50 kDa site.
source: For example, all of the CUB2/3 point mutants are more severely compromised in their ability to cleave the 33 kDa site, compared to the 50 kDa site.
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Tld cleavage of SogCR14* does not release the 33 kDa fragment.
source: Similarly, we also show that Tld cleavage of a mutant form of Sog, which is defective in Collagen IV interaction, does not release the 33 kDa fragment.
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Tsg releases the BMP-Sog-Tld complex from Collagen IV.
source: As Tsg releases the BMP-Sog-Tld complex from Collagen IV in our model, we suggest that this release involves a remodelling of protein interactions that alters the interaction of Tld with Sog allowing better access to all Sog cleavage sites, but especially the 33 kDa site, which is Tsg-dependent (Shimmi and O'Connor, 2003).
evidence: This is part of the proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: Tsg release involves a remodelling of protein interactions that alters the interaction of Tld with Sog allowing better access to all Sog cleavage sites, but especially the 33 kDa site.
source: As Tsg releases the BMP-Sog-Tld complex from Collagen IV in our model, we suggest that this release involves a remodelling of protein interactions that alters the interaction of Tld with Sog allowing better access to all Sog cleavage sites, but especially the 33 kDa site, which is Tsg-dependent (Shimmi and O'Connor, 2003).
evidence: This is speculated based on the model and supported by citation to Shimmi and O'Connor, 2003.

claim: Tld can cleave the 50 kDa Sog site when the BMP-Sog-Tld complex is bound to Collagen IV.
source: Moreover, we speculate that Tld can cleave the 50 kDa Sog site, that does not require Tsg, when the BMP-Sog-Tld complex is bound to Collagen IV, although the dual binding of Tld to Collagen IV and Sog holds Tld in a conformation that prevents both processing at the 33 kDa site and inactivation of Sog, prior to Tsg release.
evidence: This is speculated based on the differential effects on the two cleavage sites.

claim: The dual binding of Tld to Collagen IV and Sog holds Tld in a conformation that prevents both processing at the 33 kDa site and inactivation of Sog, prior to Tsg release.
source: Moreover, we speculate that Tld can cleave the 50 kDa Sog site, that does not require Tsg, when the BMP-Sog-Tld complex is bound to Collagen IV, although the dual binding of Tld to Collagen IV and Sog holds Tld in a conformation that prevents both processing at the 33 kDa site and inactivation of Sog, prior to Tsg release.
evidence: This is speculated based on the model of Tld-Sog-Collagen IV interactions.

claim: Cleavage at the 33 kDa site within Sog is necessary for complete loss of Sog inhibition of Dpp-Scw.
source: If these assumptions are correct, it follows that cleavage at the 33 kDa site within Sog is necessary for complete loss of Sog inhibition of Dpp-Scw.
evidence: This is inferred from the model and experimental observations.

claim: The Sog C-terminal fragments generated by cleavage at the other two sites retain some BMP inhibitory activity when assayed in the Drosophila wing.
source: In support of this, the Sog C-terminal fragments generated by cleavage at the other two sites retain some BMP inhibitory activity when assayed in the Drosophila wing (Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2004.

claim: Complete cleavage of Chordin is required for relief of BMP inhibition.
source: In addition, complete cleavage of Chordin, the mammalian Sog ortholog, is required for relief of BMP inhibition (Troilo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Troilo et al., 2014.

claim: Cleavage at the 33 kDa equivalent cleavage fragment of the Sog-zipper fusion protein is the preferred site.
source: We also note that although our zipper system can rescue BMP signalling thresholds in the embryo, cleavage at the 33 kDa equivalent cleavage fragment of the Sog-zipper fusion protein is the preferred site, consistent with cleavage at this site being key to full release of the Sog inhibitory effect.
evidence: This is based on cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: If in tsg mutants Tld is unable to completely release the BMP inhibition of Sog, this may explain the only partial rescue of tsg mutants by overexpression of Supersog.
source: In addition, if in tsg mutants Tld is unable to completely release the BMP inhibition of Sog, this may explain the only partial rescue of tsg mutants by overexpression of Supersog (Yu et al., 2000).
evidence: This is speculated based on the model and supported by citation to Yu et al., 2000.

claim: Supersog consists mainly of the Sog CR1 domain.
source: Supersog consists mainly of the Sog CR1 domain and has been suggested, like Tsg, to compete with full-length Sog for binding to Collagen IV to release the shuttling complex (Sawala et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawala et al., 2012.

claim: Supersog has been suggested to compete with full-length Sog for binding to Collagen IV to release the shuttling complex.
source: Supersog consists mainly of the Sog CR1 domain and has been suggested, like Tsg, to compete with full-length Sog for binding to Collagen IV to release the shuttling complex (Sawala et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sawala et al., 2012.

claim: Incomplete processing of Sog by Tld in the absence of Tsg may not relieve full inhibition of the BMP ligands.
source: However, it may be that incomplete processing of Sog by Tld in the absence of Tsg does not relieve full inhibition of the BMP ligands.
evidence: This is speculated based on the model of Tsg function.

claim: Tsg has a Sog-independent positive role with respect to BMP signalling.
source: Such a role for Tsg would be in addition to the Sog-independent positive role with respect to BMP signalling that has also been described (Wang and Ferguson, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang and Ferguson, 2005.

claim: Mutations in CUB1-2 and CUB4-5 reduce Collagen IV and Sog binding, respectively, resulting in lower levels of Sog cleavage.
source: Mutations in CUB1-2 and CUB4-5 reduce Collagen IV and Sog binding, respectively, resulting in lower levels of Sog cleavage.
evidence: This is based on the combined experimental data from binding and cleavage assays.

claim: Decreased Sog cleavage disrupts formation of the Dpp activity gradient resulting in ventralisation.
source: As the shuttle-transport mechanism relies on cycles of complex diffusion, destruction and reformation, decreased Sog cleavage disrupts formation of the Dpp activity gradient resulting in ventralisation.
evidence: This is inferred from the mechanism of BMP gradient formation and the phenotypes of tld mutants.

claim: The ΔCUB2 mutant is conformationally different so it can bind to Sog without prior presentation by Collagen IV.
source: We suggest that the ΔCUB2 mutant is conformationally different so it can bind to Sog without prior presentation by Collagen IV, but cleavage is affected, especially of the 33 kDa fragment, and not enhanced by Tsg, which may reflect perturbation of the Tld–Sog interaction, as proposed above.
evidence: This is speculated based on the differential behavior of ΔCUB2 compared to CUB2 point mutants.

claim: The CUB2 point mutant tld alleles have been shown to be antimorphic when transheterozygous with either weak tld or dpp alleles.
source: The CUB2 point mutant tld alleles have been shown to be antimorphic when transheterozygous with either weak tld or dpp alleles (Ferguson and Anderson, 1992; Finelli et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferguson and Anderson, 1992 and Finelli et al., 1994.

claim: Revertants of antimorphic tld mutations have been identified within the CUB1, 2 and 5 domains.
source: Revertants of these antimorphic mutations have also been identified within the CUB1, 2 and 5 domains (Childs and O'Connor, 1994), but as they reduce secretion of the mutant Tld proteins (Lee et al., 2009), they provide only limited insight into the molecular mechanism of the antimorphic mutants.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Childs and O'Connor, 1994 and Lee et al., 2009.

claim: Drosophila and vertebrate Tld CUB1/2 or CUB4/5 domain pairs can bind BMP4 and BMP7.
source: Nevertheless, based on the finding that Drosophila and vertebrate Tld CUB1/2 or CUB4/5 domain pairs can bind BMP4 and BMP7, and inhibit BMP signalling when injected into Xenopus embryos (with reciprocal inhibition of Tld by BMP interaction), it was proposed that the antimorphic effect of tld alleles may be due to an inhibition of Dpp activity (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: Drosophila and vertebrate Tld CUB1/2 or CUB4/5 domain pairs inhibit BMP signalling when injected into Xenopus embryos.
source: Nevertheless, based on the finding that Drosophila and vertebrate Tld CUB1/2 or CUB4/5 domain pairs can bind BMP4 and BMP7, and inhibit BMP signalling when injected into Xenopus embryos (with reciprocal inhibition of Tld by BMP interaction), it was proposed that the antimorphic effect of tld alleles may be due to an inhibition of Dpp activity (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: It was proposed that the antimorphic effect of tld alleles may be due to an inhibition of Dpp activity.
source: Nevertheless, based on the finding that Drosophila and vertebrate Tld CUB1/2 or CUB4/5 domain pairs can bind BMP4 and BMP7, and inhibit BMP signalling when injected into Xenopus embryos (with reciprocal inhibition of Tld by BMP interaction), it was proposed that the antimorphic effect of tld alleles may be due to an inhibition of Dpp activity (Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2009.

claim: Only point mutants in the CUB2 or protease domains behave in an antimorphic manner.
source: However, the role of the Tld-BMP interaction in the Drosophila embryo is not fully understood and only point mutants in the CUB2 or protease domains behave in an antimorphic manner (Ferguson and Anderson, 1992; Finelli et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferguson and Anderson, 1992 and Finelli et al., 1994.

claim: Tld and Dpp binding to Collagen IV largely prevents a direct Tld–Dpp interaction.
source: One possibility is that Tld and Dpp binding to Collagen IV largely prevents a direct Tld–Dpp interaction, but instead favours shuttling complex assembly in the presence of Sog and Tsg.
evidence: This is speculated based on the model of protein interactions.

claim: In the absence of Collagen IV binding, the CUB2 point mutants could inhibit Dpp to some extent.
source: In the absence of Collagen IV binding, the CUB2 point mutants could inhibit Dpp to some extent, further reducing Dpp activity that is already compromised in a background heterozygous for a weak tld or dpp allele.
evidence: This is speculated as a possible explanation for the antimorphic effect.

claim: The differential specificity of Tolloid non-catalytic domains, and in particular ECM interaction, may be relevant to the fine tuning of Tolloid activity in a wide range of developmental contexts.
source: The differential specificity of Tolloid non-catalytic domains, and in particular ECM interaction, may be relevant to the fine tuning of Tolloid activity not only during BMP gradient formation in other organisms, but also in a wide range of developmental contexts in general.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings in this study.

claim: In Xenopus embryos, the Chordin/BMP ligand gradient diffuses within the Fibronectin-rich Brachet's cleft.
source: In Xenopus embryos, the Chordin/BMP ligand gradient diffuses within the Fibronectin-rich Brachet's cleft (Plouhinec et al., 2013), and Fibronectin has also been shown to bind to Chordin and BMP1, to enhance the processing of Chordin during DV patterning of vertebrate embryos (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Plouhinec et al., 2013.

claim: Fibronectin has been shown to bind to Chordin and BMP1, to enhance the processing of Chordin during DV patterning of vertebrate embryos.
source: In Xenopus embryos, the Chordin/BMP ligand gradient diffuses within the Fibronectin-rich Brachet's cleft (Plouhinec et al., 2013), and Fibronectin has also been shown to bind to Chordin and BMP1, to enhance the processing of Chordin during DV patterning of vertebrate embryos (Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2009.

claim: ONT1 facilitates Chordin-BMP1 interaction by independently recruiting both proteins, resulting in robust BMP gradient formation during embryonic DV patterning.
source: Similarly, ONT1, a secreted Olfactomedin-class protein, facilitates Chordin-BMP1 interaction by independently recruiting both proteins, resulting in robust BMP gradient formation during embryonic DV patterning.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: For procollagen III processing by BMP1 in the presence of PCPE-1, heparin-like sulphated glycosaminoglycans may act as a scaffold for BMP1 processing of procollagen III in vivo.
source: In addition, for procollagen III processing by BMP1 in the presence of PCPE-1, heparin-like sulphated glycosaminoglycans may act as a scaffold for BMP1 processing of procollagen III in vivo (Bekhouche et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bekhouche et al., 2010.

claim: Tld family members may generally rely on a scaffold to facilitate substrate interaction.
source: Therefore, Tld family members may generally rely on a scaffold to facilitate substrate interaction, as proposed here for Collagen IV.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings in this study and comparison with other systems.

claim: BMP1 cleavage of Chordin is independent of BMPs.
source: Perhaps this would allow too much turnover of Chordin in vivo given that BMP1 cleavage of Chordin is independent of BMPs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of BMP1 function.

claim: BMP1 MP domain tethering would prevent interaction with secreted Frizzled-related proteins.
source: In addition, BMP1 MP domain tethering would prevent interaction with secreted Frizzled-related proteins, which are recruited via the non-catalytic domains of mammalian Tolloids to mediate important further positive and negative control of activity in specific regions of vertebrate embryos (Muraoka et al., 2006; Kobayashi et al., 2009; Ploper et al., 2011; De Robertis and Colozza, 2013; Inomata et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculated based on the known functions of secreted Frizzled-related proteins and supported by citations.

claim: Secreted Frizzled-related proteins are recruited via the non-catalytic domains of mammalian Tolloids to mediate important further positive and negative control of activity in specific regions of vertebrate embryos.
source: In addition, BMP1 MP domain tethering would prevent interaction with secreted Frizzled-related proteins, which are recruited via the non-catalytic domains of mammalian Tolloids to mediate important further positive and negative control of activity in specific regions of vertebrate embryos (Muraoka et al., 2006; Kobayashi et al., 2009; Ploper et al., 2011; De Robertis and Colozza, 2013; Inomata et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muraoka et al., 2006; Kobayashi et al., 2009; Ploper et al., 2011; De Robertis and Colozza, 2013; Inomata et al., 2013.

claim: Drosophila lacks secreted Frizzled-related proteins.
source: It is interesting that Drosophila lacks secreted Frizzled-related proteins, suggesting that ECM control of the Tld-substrate interaction is sufficient for fine control of Tld activity and the resulting Sog and BMP levels in the Drosophila embryo.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Drosophila genetics.

claim: ECM control of the Tld-substrate interaction is sufficient for fine control of Tld activity and the resulting Sog and BMP levels in the Drosophila embryo.
source: It is interesting that Drosophila lacks secreted Frizzled-related proteins, suggesting that ECM control of the Tld-substrate interaction is sufficient for fine control of Tld activity and the resulting Sog and BMP levels in the Drosophila embryo.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of secreted Frizzled-related proteins in Drosophila.

claim: Tld processing of Sog being BMP-dependent in Drosophila favours the steep BMP gradient required in this context.
source: This may stem from Tld processing of Sog being BMP-dependent in Drosophila, a situation that has already been shown to favour the steep BMP gradient required in this context (Peluso et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peluso et al., 2011.

claim: The leucine zipper system will be useful for determining sufficiency of other interactions.
source: Given that the leucine zipper system mediates an interaction between two different proteins synthesised in distinct regions of the embryo, we suggest that it will be useful for not only determining sufficiency of other interactions, but also for determining the effect of mediating ectopic or prolonged interactions between other test proteins in vivo.
evidence: This is speculated based on the success of the leucine zipper system in this study.

claim: The leucine zipper system will be useful for determining the effect of mediating ectopic or prolonged interactions between other test proteins in vivo.
source: Given that the leucine zipper system mediates an interaction between two different proteins synthesised in distinct regions of the embryo, we suggest that it will be useful for not only determining sufficiency of other interactions, but also for determining the effect of mediating ectopic or prolonged interactions between other test proteins in vivo.
evidence: This is speculated based on the success of the leucine zipper system in this study.
